visual_features.distinctive_marks: prominent dark markings on the head and carapace
visual_features.pattern: complex, irregular markings on the carapace

description: Unlike other members of its family, green turtles are mostly herbivorous when fully grown, feeding primarily on seagrasses and algae. They are the only aquatic turtle species that is herbivorous as adults. Adults usually inhabit shallow lagoons and seagrass beds. Like other sea turtles, they migrate long distances between feeding grounds and nesting beaches. Females crawl out on beaches, dig nests, and lay eggs during the night. Hatchlings emerge about two months later and scramble into the water. Those that reach maturity may live 80-90 years in the wild. The common name refers to the green fat beneath its carapace, due to its seagrass diet, not the shell color.
population_estimate: Global population increased by over 28% since the 1970s. In October 2025, the IUCN reclassified the green turtle from Endangered to Least Concern, making it one of the most dramatic recoveries on the Red List. Notable recoveries documented in nesting populations across Mexico, Hawaii, Brazil, and other key regions. Some subpopulations remain threatened, including Mediterranean green turtles facing small nesting populations and heavy coastal tourism pressure.
habitat: Inhabits tropical and subtropical waters worldwide. Adults forage primarily in seagrass beds and shallow coastal waters. Nesting occurs on sandy beaches in tropical regions. The species requires both productive seagrass feeding grounds and safe, undisturbed nesting beaches to complete its life cycle. Green turtles migrate up to thousands of kilometers between feeding areas and nesting beaches. The coral islands of the Berau Archipelago in Indonesia form one of the largest nesting sites for this species in the country.
threats: Coastal development destroying nesting beaches and seagrass habitats
Bycatch in commercial and artisanal fishing gear
Plastic pollution causing ingestion and entanglement
Climate change affecting nesting beach temperatures and sex ratios
Illegal hunting of turtles and collection of eggs
Light pollution disorienting hatchlings on nesting beaches
Boat strikes in busy coastal waters
ecosystem_role: As herbivorous grazers, green turtles play a crucial role in maintaining seagrass bed health. Their grazing promotes new seagrass growth, maintains productivity, and helps cycle nutrients. Healthy seagrass beds sequester carbon, stabilize sediments, and provide nursery habitat for countless marine species. Green turtles also transport nutrients between marine and terrestrial ecosystems through their nesting activities, fertilizing coastal vegetation with their eggs and hatchling shells.
human_connection: Green turtles have deep cultural significance for coastal communities worldwide and feature prominently in the mythology of many indigenous cultures. Their dramatic recovery from Endangered to Least Concern in 2025 demonstrates the power of coordinated international conservation. They are protected under CITES Appendix I since 1988 and are legally protected in most countries. The species' recovery is a conservation success story, but continued vigilance is needed as some regional populations remain at risk from coastal development, illegal hunting, and climate change.
what_students_can_do: Reduce plastic use to prevent marine debris that entangles turtles
Support sea turtle conservation programs through reputable organizations
Choose sustainable seafood to reduce bycatch impact on turtles
Participate in beach cleanups and report injured turtles to local authorities
Reduce light pollution during nesting season if living near turtle beaches
Learn about and support the Marine Turtle Conservation Fund
fun_fact: Green turtles can hold their breath for up to 5 hours while resting under ledges
They return to the exact beach where they were born to nest, sometimes traveling thousands of miles across oceans
Nest temperature determines hatchling sex: warmer sand produces more females, cooler sand produces more males
Green sea turtles have been swimming the oceans for over 100 million years since the time of the dinosaurs
In October 2025, the IUCN officially downlisted the green turtle from Endangered to Least Concern—one of the most dramatic conservation recoveries on the Red List
